title: Bad COP, worse COP: what COP31 left Bangladesh
excerpt: COP31 dropped the adaptation finance target Bangladesh backed. It came home with Tk 784 crore in grants and another year of relying on loans.

image.alt: Campaigners hold a banner reading FAILURE inside the COP31 venue in Antalya, Türkiye

content:
DHAKA, 27 November 2026: Bangladesh returned from the UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, with about Tk 784 crore in new grants but none of the global commitments it sought, after COP31 collapsed without a final agreement.

The proposal to triple adaptation finance to US$120 billion a year by 2035, which Bangladesh supported, appeared in none of the final texts, according to Carbon Brief. No target was set for the loss and damage fund, and debt relief was not discussed in any decision.

The outcome leaves Bangladesh's funding gap unchanged. The country needs about $8.5 billion a year for adaptation and receives less than $0.5 billion of it from international sources, according to figures released by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) during the summit.

This explainer sets out what Bangladesh asked for, what the talks produced, why they failed, and what the result means for the government, NGOs and the communities that depend on adaptation funding. The next opportunity to revive the adaptation target is COP32, to be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in November 2027.

What Bangladesh asked for

Bangladesh's central demand at COP31 was that money for adaptation and for loss and damage should come as grants rather than loans. It was the first UN climate summit for the government that took office in February, and ministers repeated the demand throughout the two weeks.

The delegation set out six main demands between 9 and 17 November:

  1. Three times more adaptation finance. Bangladesh backed the call by the Least Developed Countries (LDC) group to triple adaptation finance to $120 billion a year before 2035.
  2. Half of climate finance for adaptation. In his national statement on 12 November, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman asked that at least 50% of international climate finance go to adaptation, The Business Standard reported. The demand sets a share of all climate finance rather than a fixed sum.
  3. Grants, not loans. "Climate-vulnerable countries need grants, not more loans that increase their debt," the Prime Minister said. He also called for debt-for-climate swaps and climate-resilient debt clauses.
  4. A loss and damage fund that pays out. The delegation asked for more money, simpler access and faster payments, including for non-economic losses, at a press briefing on 13 November.
  5. Direct access to climate funds. It asked for simpler routes into the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Adaptation Fund, and more support for locally led adaptation.
  6. A just transition mechanism. The Prime Minister asked for the mechanism to be adopted at COP31, with fair finance and trade at its core.

The demands rested on the size of the gap. Officials told the 13 November briefing that Bangladesh needs $10 billion to $11 billion a year for all climate action and pays $4.5 billion to $5 billion of it from its own budget. For adaptation alone, UNDP put the need at about $8.5 billion a year. About $4 billion is available, and less than $0.5 billion of it comes from abroad.

Bangladesh did not put a figure on compensation. "Negotiations do not work around a single pre-set compensation sum," Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo said before the talks, bdnews24.com reported.

What COP31 decided, and what it dropped

The talks closed at 7:33pm local time on Sunday, 22 November, nearly 50 hours behind schedule, making COP31 the longest UN climate summit on record, according to Carbon Brief. The cover decision, informally called the "Antalya pact", was rejected in the closing plenary. Several technical decisions were adopted.

Outside the negotiations, Bangladesh secured two grants. Dr Saimum Parvez, special assistant to the Prime Minister on environment, forest and climate change, told reporters in Dhaka on 22 November that the Climate Investment Funds would provide US$30 million and the Global Shield against Climate Risks €30 million, together about Tk 784 crore, Daily Waadaa reported. A further €20 million from the Global Shield depends on the first phase being carried out successfully. None of the money has to be repaid, he said.

The money gap, in numbers

By UNDP's figures, the shortfall between Bangladesh's adaptation needs and international funding is about $8 billion a year. Nearly 88% of the adaptation money the country spends comes from its own budget, and much of what arrives from abroad comes as loans.

Two comparisons show the scale of the new grants. Bareesh Hasan Chowdhury, policy and campaigns coordinator at the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA), estimated the grants Bangladesh obtained at $60 million to $100 million, about 1% or less of a year's National Adaptation Plan needs, Daily Waadaa reported. And by Devlens' calculation, the global loss and damage fund's total pledges of $342 million are less than Bangladesh's adaptation need for three weeks.

The global gap is of the same order. Developed countries provided $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in public adaptation finance to developing countries in 2024, according to the UN Environment Programme's (UNEP) Adaptation Gap Report 2026, as reported by allAfrica. UNEP puts developing countries' adaptation needs at $305 billion a year by 2035, Carbon Brief reported. Even the dropped $120 billion target would have covered only 20% to 29% of those needs, by UNEP's estimate.

Why loans matter. Adaptation money that arrives as loans must be repaid from the national budget. Bangladesh received $2.70 in climate-related loans for every $1 in grants, according to the Climate Debt Risk Index published by the Dhaka think tank Change Initiative in November 2025. The same study counted $3.4 billion in climate-related loans between 2009 and 2022, against $1.41 billion received for adaptation between 2002 and 2023. Bangladesh is due to graduate from LDC status in 2029, which could reduce its access to concessional finance, Daily Waadaa noted.

Why the talks failed

The adaptation finance target, Bangladesh's main demand, depended on the cover decision. When that text collapsed in a dispute over fossil fuels, the target fell with it.

The fossil fuel dispute. The first draft of the cover decision, issued on 16 November, called for faster action to phase out fossil fuels. The second draft dropped the reference. On the final Saturday, 126 countries, including the LDC group with which Bangladesh negotiates, asked the presidency to restore it, according to Carbon Brief. Saudi Arabia was "vehemently opposed", AFP reported, and Russia opposed "any wording on fossil fuels". The final draft only "recalled" the COP28 agreement. "We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels," the European Union said. Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu were among at least 32 countries that rejected the text, Carbon Brief reported.

The finance dispute. The African Group of Negotiators' request for a separate agenda item on tripling adaptation finance was refused on the first day, after the EU signalled it would not accept one, allAfrica reported. Negotiators then divided over the baseline year. Developing countries proposed 2025, which would give $120 billion; France, co-chairing the ministerial finance talks, reportedly proposed 2019, which would halve the target to $60 billion, according to Carbon Brief. Neither figure survived. "Rich countries won't provide enough climate finance to the developing world," Frank Jotzo, professor of environmental and climate change economics at the Australian National University, told AFP.

What the rejected text said. The final draft had already moved away from a number. An earlier version called for "efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035" with a $120 billion goal, ABC News reported. The last version only "agrees to discuss … implementation pathways for tripling adaptation finance by 2035", and on loss and damage it "encourages continued efforts to scale up" funding. Even had the text been adopted, Bangladesh would not have secured a figure. Al Jazeera reported that the wars in Iran and Ukraine have strained the budgets of the countries expected to provide the money.

The consensus rule. UN climate decisions require the agreement of every country. "Decision-making that requires every country to agree on every comma is not fit for a climate emergency," Nikki Reisch of the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL) told AFP. Chris Bowen, Australia's climate minister, who chaired the negotiations, called the result "very disappointing" and pointed to the same rule, adding that "you also need consensus to change consensus".

International reaction. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the outcome "deeply disappointing". "There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science," he said, calling for stronger support for vulnerable countries and a substantial increase in adaptation finance, UN News reported. "You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs," Sebastien Duyck of CIEL told Al Jazeera. Before the talks opened, the chair of the 44-member LDC group, Ambassador Adão Soares Barbosa of Timor-Leste, had warned: "COP31 cannot be another exercise in deferring difficult decisions."

In Bangladesh, analysts differed on the scale of the setback. "COP31's failure does not immediately cost Bangladesh a deal; it costs Bangladesh a year," M Zakir Hossain Khan, chief executive of Change Initiative, told Daily Waadaa. Bareesh Hasan Chowdhury of BELA cautioned against calling the whole conference a failure, while describing the sums on offer as "beyond inadequate". Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, told the same newspaper: "No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure."

Why it matters for NGOs and communities

Much of Bangladesh's climate adaptation work, from embankments and cyclone shelters to salt-tolerant farming, safe water and early warning, is delivered by NGOs in coastal districts, char lands and haor wetlands. Many of these programmes rely on donor grants, which have fallen sharply since 2025. COP31 offers no new source of grant money to replace them.

In Devlens' reading, the result has three practical consequences for the sector.

  1. No new global benchmark for donors. Without an adaptation finance target, donors face no new commitment to measure against. Organisations planning 2027 budgets have little basis to expect growth in climate grants.
  2. New money is small and channelled through government. The Global Shield grant supports climate risk finance, including insurance, and the Climate Investment Funds grant is channelled through the government, Dr Parvez said. NGOs seeking a role will need to know which ministry and programme holds each grant.
  3. No funding decision for locally led adaptation. The delegation asked for more support for locally led adaptation, but no COP31 decision attached money to it. The Adaptation Fund's new share of carbon-market revenue may widen direct access for national bodies over time.

Coastal communities had set out their position before the talks ended. Women and fishers formed a human chain on the bank of the Pashur river in Mongla to demand that climate finance come as grants, The Daily Star reported on 17 November. "Climate finance must not become another burden of debt," climate activist Ratna Sheikh said. Speakers asked for a say when the National Adaptation Plan and Bangladesh's climate pledges are next revised.

Some analysts argue that Bangladesh should not rely on the COP process alone. "The answer is not to abandon the COP, but to stop depending on it alone," Zakir Hossain Khan of Change Initiative told Daily Waadaa. He proposed a coalition of climate-vulnerable, debt-burdened countries and a South Asian Resilience Fund modelled on Pacific schemes.

What to watch

The adaptation finance target will return at COP32 in Addis Ababa in November 2027. "We hope it will be decided at the next COP," Mirza Shawkat Ali, director of climate change and international conventions at the Department of Environment, told Daily Waadaa. The key dates for Bangladesh before then are set out below.

Two routes outside the COP process are drawing more attention, AFP reported. The first is international law. An advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice has confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to act on climate change. "If the negotiations are not delivering what individual states need, then they'll certainly consider turning to the ICJ and other international courts," said Harj Narulla, an international lawyer who advised the Solomon Islands at COP31.

The second is agreement among willing countries. The Santa Marta initiative, launched after COP30, brings together countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels; 57 countries met under it in April, Al Jazeera reported. Jotzo said such groupings are growing and that more are needed, including on adaptation finance. Bowen said Santa Marta "doesn't replace COP. It's just another way of doing it."

At home: how the government uses the Tk 784 crore in grants and which agencies manage them; whether the review of the National Adaptation Plan includes coastal community groups; and whether Bangladesh's next climate pledge, its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), sets aside a share of adaptation work for local delivery.

About this explainer

This Devlens explainer was prepared by the Devlens Editorial Team. It draws on the record of final decisions published by Carbon Brief; reporting by UN News, AFP, Al Jazeera and ABC News; the UNDP release on Bangladesh's adaptation finance; statements by the LDC group; and Bangladeshi press coverage from 9 to 25 November 2026. Facts are attributed to their sources. Assessments, including the comparison of Bangladesh's demands with the outcome, are Devlens' own and are marked as such. Graphics are by Devlens Bangladesh.

Notes on the figures. Reports differ on the Global Shield grant; some put it at €50 million. This report uses the figures Dr Saimum Parvez gave on 22 November: €30 million confirmed and a further €20 million subject to results. The adaptation need of $8.5 billion a year is taken from a UNDP release; Devlens has not seen the government estimate behind it. Dollar figures are US dollars.
